Penelope Packrat was very pleased with herself. "It is the most beautiful thing I have ever found!" she declared to no one in particular. She was scurrying home along the edge of Briar-Rose Creek, dragging a small, shiny object. It was a little silver bell, and it made a delightful *tinkle-tinkle-tinkle* sound as she pulled it over the pebbles.

Once inside her cozy den, however, the bell became a nuisance. Every time Penelope moved a pebble or rearranged her collection of bottle-caps, the bell would jingle loudly. "Oh, be quiet!" she snapped at it. But the bell, of course, did not listen. It tinkled when she went to get a drink, and it tinkled when she lay down to rest.

"This will never do," she finally decided. "A collector needs peace and quiet!"

The next morning, she pushed the bell outside her den and went to find Chatterton Sparrow, who was busy arguing with a caterpillar. "Mr. Sparrow," she began, "I have a gift for you."

"A gift!" Chatterton chirped, hopping from one foot to the other. "What is it? Is it a juicy worm?"

"No, indeed!" Penelope replied. "It is something much better. It is a silver singing-stone."

She led him to the bell. Chatterton Sparrow cocked his head and looked at it. "A singing-stone!" he repeated. He pecked it with his beak, and it let out a sharp *ting*. "It's very loud," he said. "And I think it is far too heavy for my nest. I thank you for the offer, but I would have no use for it."

Penelope Packrat sighed. Next, she went to find Bertram Badger, who was digging for roots near an old stump. "Mr. Badger," she said, "do you have a use for a warning device?"

Bertram Badger looked up from his work, dirt on his nose. "A warning device?" he grumbled. "I am my own warning device. What are you talking about?"

"I have found a bell," Penelope explained. "It makes a noise whenever danger is near." This, of course, was not exactly true, but Penelope was getting desperate.

"Hmph," said Bertram. "Let me see this thing." He followed her to the bell and nudged it with his great nose. *Tinkle-tinkle*. "That's no warning bell," he announced gruffly. "You are a silly creature, Penelope Packrat. Any one with any sense can see this is a _dinner_ bell. You ring it when your supper is ready."

"You didn't say so," Penelope said. "You just saw it now."

"That--" said Bertram Badger--"that is because I have worldly knowledge. I suppose you thought it was a shiny mushroom. Now, if you will excuse me, I must get back to my work." And he lumbered off, leaving Penelope alone with the noisy bell.

But Bertram Badger did not keep his worldly knowledge to himself. He told Willow Weasel that he had discovered a proper dinner bell. And Willow Weasel told Timothy Mouse. And Timothy Mouse told the Rabbit cousins. By the time the story had made its way all through the deep woods, it had changed a good deal.

This is what Penelope Packrat heard from Chatterton Sparrow later that day: Bertram Badger was having a party. He had dug up enough sweet roots and wild carrots to feed every single animal in the wood. And he was going to ring his new dinner bell at sundown to call them all to the feast.

Penelope was surprised. "A feast?" she said. "He told me he was busy."

"It's a surprise feast!" Chatterton chirped. "Everyone is going!"

So just as the sun began to set, a great crowd of animals gathered quietly near Bertram Badger's den. They waited and waited. At last, Bertram came out. He saw the crowd and scowled. "What is all this?" he bellowed. "Why are you all lurking about my home?"

Timothy Mouse squeaked bravely. "For the feast, Mr. Badger. For the great dinner-bell feast."

"Feast!" Bertram Badger roared. "There is no feast! Who told you such a foolish story?"

Just then, Penelope Packrat pushed her way to the front. "I believe it is my fault," she said quietly. She explained all about the noisy bell, and what Bertram had called it.

Bertram Badger's face turned quite red. "Well," he sputtered, "I only said what it _looked_ like. I never said I was providing the dinner!"

The animals all looked very disappointed. "But just think of all the roots you have," Timothy Mouse reminded him.

Bertram Badger shook his head. "I'm afraid I'm too busy to host a party," he told the crowd.

"Then--" Penelope said--"then how do we know what you say is true when you tell us something is a dinner bell?"

And Bertram Badger could find no answer to that. He was embarrassed, too. For he was afraid he would have to share his roots, after all.

"Well, what's this?" he said aloud. He picked it up and smoothed it out. There was the envelope with the picture of the chipmunk in the corner. And there was the paper from inside, with its pictures of a squirrel, a mouse, and a rat. Johnnie Green began to laugh all over again.

"It's from the seed company!" he exclaimed. "It's the new catalog!" He saw at once why Sandy Chipmunk had been so certain the letter was his. The picture in the corner was the trademark for "Chipmunk's Choice Sunflower Seeds." And the pictures inside were advertisements for other kinds of seeds, meant for other creatures.

When he got back to the house, he showed the catalog to his father. "Here is the important letter, Father," he said, with a twinkle in his eye. "I found it in the road."

Farmer Green put on his spectacles and looked at the paper. A slow smile spread across his face. "Well, I'll be," he said. "So that's what all the fuss was about. That chipmunk thought he was getting mail." He handed the paper back to Johnnie. "I suppose there's no harm done, then. But it's a lesson to that little scamp not to meddle with things that don't belong to him."

But Johnnie Green thought it was the finest joke in the world. And he began to form a little plan in his head. It seemed a shame for Sandy Chipmunk to be so disappointed after thinking he had received a real letter.

XIII A SECRET MESSAGE

The next morning, Mr. Crow was still thinking about the letter. He had convinced himself that Sandy Chipmunk must have crept back and taken it. "He tricked me!" Mr. Crow grumbled to himself. "He pretended to throw it away, just so I would leave. Then he scurried back to read his secrets alone."

This thought made Mr. Crow feel very sly and clever, for he believed he had uncovered a plot. So he flew straight to the stone wall where Sandy Chipmunk made his home.

"You're a clever one, aren't you?" Mr. Crow began without even a "Good morning."

Sandy Chipmunk, who was just polishing his whiskers after a breakfast of last year's acorns, looked up in surprise. "I don't know what you mean, Mr. Crow," he said.

"Oh, yes you do!" Mr. Crow cawed. "You and your secret letter! You thought you could fool me, but you can't. I know you went back for it. What was in it? Was it a map to a hidden store of corn?" Mr. Crow's eyes gleamed at the thought.

"I did no such thing!" Sandy Chipmunk replied, and his tail twitched with irritation. "I threw the letter away because _you_ told me it was no good. I haven't seen it since."

"A likely story!" Mr. Crow sneered. "I suppose the wind just carried it off to a secret hiding place for you."

And though Mr. Crow had meant it as a joke, that is exactly what had happened, in a way. But Sandy did not know that. He only knew that Mr. Crow was being disagreeable again. "I have no secret, and no letter," Sandy said firmly. "And now if you'll excuse me, I have winter nuts to gather."

Mr. Crow flew off in a huff, certain that he was being lied to. He was so busy muttering to himself that he nearly flew right into Jasper Jay.

"What's the trouble, Mr. Crow?" Jasper asked. "You look as if you've lost your breakfast."

"Worse than that," Mr. Crow said, puffing out his chest. "Sandy Chipmunk is holding out on us. He received a secret message in the mail-box. A map, I believe. It probably leads to a whole crib full of Farmer Green's corn."

Well, Jasper Jay was a terrible gossip. And he could not wait to tell some one this exciting news. He flew off and told Frisky Squirrel. But when he told the story, it had grown a little. "Sandy Chipmunk has a treasure map," he said. "It came in the mail. And it shows the way to a mountain of corn and a river of molasses."

Frisky Squirrel told his cousin. And his cousin told Fatty Coon. And the story traveled and grew, until it was really quite grand. By the time it came back to Sandy Chipmunk himself, as he was busy burying a beechnut, it was quite unbelievable. It was Timothy Mouse who told him.

"Is it true, Sandy?" Timothy squeaked, his eyes wide. "Did you really get a map from a king who lives in the village? And does it truly lead to a castle made of cheese?"

Sandy Chipmunk just stared. "A castle made of cheese?" he repeated slowly. "I'm afraid you have been listening to Mr. Crow again." And he shook his head and went back to his work, wondering how things in Pleasant Valley always seemed to get so twisted.

Meanwhile, Johnnie Green had decided to put his plan into action. He took a nice, plump hickory nut from his pocket. Then he found a tiny scrap of paper and, with a pencil, drew a picture of a smiling face on it. He tied the little paper to the nut with a bit of red thread.

He walked down to the cross-roads, and then along the stone wall until he came to the hole that led to Sandy's home. Very carefully, he placed the hickory nut, with its little paper flag, right at the entrance. "There," he whispered. "A special delivery for Mr. Chipmunk." Then he ran back to the farmhouse to watch from his window.

XIV A PUZZLING GIFT

When Sandy Chipmunk returned to his doorstep, tired from a long morning of work, the first thing he saw was the hickory nut. It was a fine nut, bigger and smoother than most. But it was the little paper tied to it that made him stop and stare.

He crept closer. He sniffed the nut. It smelled delicious. He nudged the paper with his nose. It fluttered in the breeze. He had never seen such a thing.

"What can this be?" he said to himself. He remembered the trouble the last piece of mail had caused him. And he was not at all sure he wanted another. Still, a hickory nut was a hickory nut. And this one had been left right at his door.

He untied the red thread with his teeth and paws. The paper fell to the ground. He looked at the drawing of the smiling face. It meant nothing to him. It was just a circle with dots and a curved line. It was a great puzzle.

Just then, Frisky Squirrel came scampering along the top of the wall. "What have you got there, Sandy?" he chattered.

"I don't know," Sandy confessed. "I found it here. It's a nut with a picture tied to it."

Frisky hopped down for a closer look. He turned the paper over and over. "That's queer!" he said. "It's not a letter, for there are no words. And it's not a map, for there are no lines and arrows." He looked at the smiling face. "Perhaps it is a warning. It looks a little like the full moon. Maybe it means you should only come out at night."

"But I am not an owl or a coon," Sandy objected. "I like the daylight. It can't mean that."

The two of them sat there for a long time, looking at the nut and the paper, and they were no wiser than before.

"There is only one person who might know," Frisky said at last, though he did not like the idea. "We will have to ask Mr. Crow. He is old and claims to know all about the ways of men."

Sandy did not like the idea either. But his curiosity was even greater than his annoyance. "Very well," he sighed. "But you must come with me. He is more likely to behave himself if there is a witness."

So together they went in search of Mr. Crow. They found him perched on the highest branch of a dead chestnut tree, looking very important.

"Mr. Crow," Sandy began politely. "We have a puzzle for you."

Mr. Crow looked down his long beak at them. "I am very busy with important thoughts," he said. "But I suppose I can spare a moment for you little fellows."

Sandy held up the scrap of paper. "I found this tied to a nut at my door," he explained. "Do you know what it means?"

Mr. Crow peered at the drawing. He squinted one eye, then the other. He had no more idea what it was than Sandy did. But he would never, ever admit that. He had a reputation to maintain. He had to think of something clever.

"Hmph!" he snorted, stalling for time. He remembered his theory about Farmer Green setting traps. And he remembered the talk of maps. An idea, a truly dreadful and exciting idea, popped into his head.

"This," he announced in a grave voice, "is no smiling face. And it is no moon. You are both very foolish. Any one with any experience can see what this is. It is a picture of a _trap_."

"A trap!" Frisky and Sandy exclaimed in one breath.

"Certainly," said Mr. Crow, warming to his story. "It is one of those round, steel traps with teeth. Farmer Green has drawn you a picture of it so you will know what to look for. And he has left you a nut for bait, to show you how he will trick you. It is a warning!"

"A warning?" Sandy asked. "But... but why would he warn me?"

"That--" said Mr. Crow--"that is the cunning of it. He is playing a game with you. He is telling you, 'I am going to set this trap for you, and I dare you to avoid it.' It is a challenge! And the red thread means danger. Great danger!"

Frisky Squirrel's tail bushed out in alarm. Sandy Chipmunk felt a cold shiver run all the way down his back. A trap! A challenge from Farmer Green himself! It was a terrible thought.

"Thank you, Mr. Crow," Sandy said in a small voice. "You have been a great help."

"Of course," Mr. Crow cawed, puffing out his chest again. "Now you know. And you had better tell every one. Farmer Green is on the war-path. No nut is safe!"

XV A FOREST IN A FRIGHT

As you can imagine, that dreadful news spread through the woods and fields even faster than the story about the treasure map. Frisky Squirrel, his heart pounding with fear, scurried off to tell his family. "Farmer Green is setting steel traps everywhere!" he chattered. "He is using nuts for bait, and he leaves a picture of the trap so you know it's his! And the nuts are tied with a red thread of doom!"

The squirrel family told the Rabbit cousins. And the Rabbit cousins, who were frightened of their own shadows, told every one they met. Fatty Coon heard it and decided to stay in his hollow tree all the next day. Even bold Peter Mink, who was afraid of nothing, thought it might be wise to stick close to the river bank.

By sundown, all of Pleasant Valley was in a state of terror. The woods, usually full of the rustle and bustle of busy folk, were strangely silent. No one dared to touch a fallen nut. Every twig that snapped sounded like the clang of a trap.

Sandy Chipmunk was the most miserable of all. He hid deep in his nest, the fine hickory nut lying untouched in the corner. He felt it was all his fault. If he had never meddled with the mail-box, none of this would have happened.

The next morning, Johnnie Green was very disappointed. He had watched from his window, but he had not seen the chipmunk take the nut. "Maybe he didn't see it," he said to himself.

So, on his way to school, he left another present. This time it was a shiny brass button that had fallen off his coat. He placed it right on the flat stone that Sandy used as a porch.

When Sandy finally peeked out of his hole, there was the button, gleaming in the sun. He froze in horror. It was round, just like the drawing. It was made of metal. It must be one of the traps!

He backed into his tunnel, his heart thumping. "He knows where I live!" he whispered. "He's putting the traps right on my doorstep!"

He stayed hidden all day. He was very hungry, for he was now afraid to eat the hickory nut, too. Late in the afternoon, his hunger made him bold. He crept out and scurried to a different part of the stone wall, far from his home, where he had a secret stash of acorns. As he was digging one up, he heard a familiar voice.

"Well, well. If it isn't the fellow who started all the trouble."

It was Mr. Crow.

"It wasn't my fault," Sandy mumbled, his mouth full of acorn.

"You brought the warning," Mr. Crow insisted. "And now look. The whole valley is starving, afraid to pick up a single nut. I myself have not had a decent meal all day. There's a perfectly good field of corn over there, but who dares go near it? It is surely surrounded by those round, metal things."

Sandy Chipmunk looked over at Farmer Green's cornfield. It did look tempting. The stalks were brown, and the ears were heavy. Then he looked toward the farmhouse. He saw Johnnie Green coming out the back door. The boy was carrying a small basket.

Sandy's first instinct was to run and hide. But then his curiosity got the better of him. He stayed perfectly still behind the wall and watched.

Johnnie did not walk toward the woods. Instead, he walked to a new wooden pole that his father had put up near the garden. On top of the pole was a little house with a hole in it. Farmer Green had built it for the bluebirds.

Johnnie reached into his basket and began to fill the little house with something. It was birdseed. Then he scattered some more on the ground around the pole. He waited for a minute, and then two bluebirds flew down and began to peck at the seeds. They flew in and out of the little house, singing happily. They did not seem to be in any danger at all.

Sandy watched, his brow wrinkled in thought. He watched as Johnnie went back to the house. He watched the birds for a long, long time. They were not afraid. There was no trap.

A new idea began to form in Sandy's mind. It was a small idea at first, but it grew and grew. What if the round thing was not a trap? What if the smiling face was not a picture of a trap? What if... what if Mr. Crow had been wrong?

It was a startling thought. Mr. Crow was _always_ so sure of himself. But the more Sandy thought about it, the more sense it made. The bluebirds were safe. Johnnie Green did not look like a wicked trickster; he looked like a boy scattering seeds.

"There is only one way to be sure," Sandy said to himself. And his heart began to beat fast, not with fear this time, but with a kind of nervous courage.

He scurried back to his nest and bravely poked his head out. The brass button was still there. He nudged it. It didn't snap. It didn't bite. It just slid across the stone. He picked it up. It was smooth and cool. It was not a trap at all. It was just a button.

Then he looked at the hickory nut. He untied the red thread and nibbled one end of the nut. It was sweet and delicious. It was not poisoned.

Mr. Crow was wrong. He was completely and utterly wrong.

XVI SANDY THE BRAVE

A great anger rose in Sandy Chipmunk's chest. It was an anger at being so frightened, and at seeing all his neighbors so frightened, all for nothing.

"I must tell them," he declared. "I must tell them the truth."

He took the brass button in his mouth and scampered to the top of the stone wall. "Listen!" he squeaked as loudly as he could. "Every one, listen to me!"

A few heads popped out. Frisky Squirrel peered from a hole in a tree. A rabbit peeked from behind a bush.

"It's a trick!" a voice squawked from above. It was Mr. Crow, swooping down to land on a nearby fence post. "He has one of the traps! He is trying to lure you out! Don't listen to him!"

"It is not a trap!" Sandy cried, dropping the button so they could all see it. "It is a button! Just a plain, ordinary button! And the nut was not poisoned! It was a good nut!"

"Lies!" cawed Mr. Crow. "He is working for Farmer Green! He has turned traitor!"

The woodsfolk ducked back into their hiding places, confused and afraid. They did not know whom to believe. Sandy was their friend, but Mr. Crow was old and sounded so very certain.

Sandy knew he had to do something more. Words were not enough. He had to show them. He remembered the cornfield, and the bluebirds, and Johnnie Green. He had a daring plan.

"Follow me!" he shouted. "If you are brave enough, follow me and I will show you the truth!"

He leaped from the wall and ran, not toward the deep woods, but out into the open, straight for Farmer Green's garden and the new bluebird house. Mr. Crow and a few of the bolder animals followed at a distance, hiding behind trees and bushes, to see what would happen.

Sandy did not hesitate. He ran right up to the pole of the birdhouse. He could smell the fresh seed. His heart was in his throat, but he kept going. He scrambled up the wooden pole, just as he would climb a tree.

"He's done for now!" Mr. Crow whispered to Jasper Jay, who was shivering on a branch beside him. "It's a trap for birds and chipmunks alike!"

Sandy reached the little house. He crept onto its roof and looked down. Below, he could see the scared faces of his friends, peeking out from their hiding spots. He took a deep breath. Then he hopped down onto the little platform by the entrance hole and boldly stuck his head inside.

He grabbed a big, striped sunflower seed, one of "Chipmunk's Choice," in fact. He backed out and held it up for all to see. Then, sitting there on the platform of the birdhouse, in full view of Farmer Green's kitchen window, he ate it.

A great, collective gasp went up from the woods. They waited. They watched.

Nothing happened. Sandy Chipmunk did not fall over. The house did not snap shut on him. He simply finished his seed, wiped his whiskers, and took another.

A cheer went up from the squirrels. The rabbits thumped their feet in applause. One by one, the animals came out of hiding, their faces full of relief and wonder.

Sandy Chipmunk had been right. It was not a trap. It was a bird feeder.

All eyes turned to Mr. Crow. He sat on his fence post, his feathers ruffled. He looked from the cheering crowd to Sandy, who was now happily stuffing his cheeks with seeds. Mr. Crow had never felt so foolish in his entire life. He had been wrong about the letter, and now he had been wrong about the trap. He had frightened the entire valley for no reason at all.

Without a single _caw_ or a boast or a sneer, he spread his black wings and flew away, over the trees and out of sight.

That evening, the woods were once again full of happy sounds. The animals feasted on the nuts they had been too afraid to touch. Sandy Chipmunk, a hero, sat on his doorstep, polishing his shiny brass button. He had learned a great many things. He had learned that stories change in the telling. He had learned that the oldest and loudest person is not always the wisest.

And most important of all, he had learned that it is a fine thing to receive a letter, but it is an even finer thing to find out the truth for yourself.

This thought made Mr. Crow feel very sly and clever, for he believed he had uncovered a plot. So he flew straight to the stone wall where Sandy Chipmunk made his home.

"You're a clever one, aren't you?" Mr. Crow began without even a "Good morning."

Sandy Chipmunk, who was just polishing his whiskers after a breakfast of last year's acorns, looked up in surprise. "I don't know what you mean, Mr. Crow," he said.

"Oh, yes you do!" Mr. Crow cawed. "You and your secret letter! You thought you could fool me, but you can't. I know you went back for it. What was in it? Was it a map to a hidden store of corn?" Mr. Crow's eyes gleamed at the thought.

"I did no such thing!" Sandy Chipmunk replied, and his tail twitched with irritation. "I threw the letter away because _you_ told me it was no good. I haven't seen it since."

"A likely story!" Mr. Crow sneered. "I suppose the wind just carried it off to a secret hiding place for you."

And though Mr. Crow had meant it as a joke, that is exactly what had happened, in a way. But Sandy did not know that. He only knew that Mr. Crow was being disagreeable again. "I have no secret, and no letter," Sandy said firmly. "And now if you'll excuse me, I have winter nuts to gather."

Mr. Crow flew off in a huff, certain that he was being lied to. He was so busy muttering to himself that he nearly flew right into Jasper Jay.

"What's the trouble, Mr. Crow?" Jasper asked. "You look as if you've lost your breakfast."

"Worse than that," Mr. Crow said, puffing out his chest. "Sandy Chipmunk is holding out on us. He received a secret message in the mail-box. A map, I believe. It probably leads to a whole crib full of Farmer Green's corn."

Well, Jasper Jay was a terrible gossip. And he could not wait to tell some one this exciting news. He flew off and told Frisky Squirrel. But when he told the story, it had grown a little. "Sandy Chipmunk has a treasure map," he said. "It came in the mail. And it shows the way to a mountain of corn and a river of molasses."

Frisky Squirrel told his cousin. And his cousin told Fatty Coon. And the story traveled and grew, until it was really quite grand. By the time it came back to Sandy Chipmunk himself, as he was busy burying a beechnut, it was quite unbelievable. It was Timothy Mouse who told him.

"Is it true, Sandy?" Timothy squeaked, his eyes wide. "Did you really get a map from a king who lives in the village? And does it truly lead to a castle made of cheese?"

Sandy Chipmunk just stared. "A castle made of cheese?" he repeated slowly. "I'm afraid you have been listening to Mr. Crow again." And he shook his head and went back to his work, wondering how things in Pleasant Valley always seemed to get so twisted.

Meanwhile, Johnnie Green had decided to put his plan into action. He took a nice, plump hickory nut from his pocket. Then he found a tiny scrap of paper and, with a pencil, drew a picture of a smiling face on it. He tied the little paper to the nut with a bit of red thread.

He walked down to the cross-roads, and then along the stone wall until he came to the hole that led to Sandy's home. Very carefully, he placed the hickory nut, with its little paper flag, right at the entrance. "There," he whispered. "A special delivery for Mr. Chipmunk." Then he ran back to the farmhouse to watch from his window.

XIV A PUZZLING GIFT

When Sandy Chipmunk returned to his doorstep, tired from a long morning of work, the first thing he saw was the hickory nut. It was a fine nut, bigger and smoother than most. But it was the little paper tied to it that made him stop and stare.

He crept closer. He sniffed the nut. It smelled delicious. He nudged the paper with his nose. It fluttered in the breeze. He had never seen such a thing.

"What can this be?" he said to himself. He remembered the trouble the last piece of mail had caused him. And he was not at all sure he wanted another. Still, a hickory nut was a hickory nut. And this one had been left right at his door.

He untied the red thread with his teeth and paws. The paper fell to the ground. He looked at the drawing of the smiling face. It meant nothing to him. It was just a circle with dots and a curved line. It was a great puzzle.

Just then, Frisky Squirrel came scampering along the top of the wall. "What have you got there, Sandy?" he chattered.

"I don't know," Sandy confessed. "I found it here. It's a nut with a picture tied to it."

Frisky hopped down for a closer look. He turned the paper over and over. "That's queer!" he said. "It's not a letter, for there are no words. And it's not a map, for there are no lines and arrows." He looked at the smiling face. "Perhaps it is a warning. It looks a little like the full moon. Maybe it means you should only come out at night."

"But I am not an owl or a coon," Sandy objected. "I like the daylight. It can't mean that."

The two of them sat there for a long time, looking at the nut and the paper, and they were no wiser than before.

"There is only one person who might know," Frisky said at last, though he did not like the idea. "We will have to ask Mr. Crow. He is old and claims to know all about the ways of men."

Sandy did not like the idea either. But his curiosity was even greater than his annoyance. "Very well," he sighed. "But you must come with me. He is more likely to behave himself if there is a witness."

So together they went in search of Mr. Crow. They found him perched on the highest branch of a dead chestnut tree, looking very important.

"Mr. Crow," Sandy began politely. "We have a puzzle for you."

Mr. Crow looked down his long beak at them. "I am very busy with important thoughts," he said. "But I suppose I can spare a moment for you little fellows."

Sandy held up the scrap of paper. "I found this tied to a nut at my door," he explained. "Do you know what it means?"

Mr. Crow peered at the drawing. He squinted one eye, then the other. He had no more idea what it was than Sandy did. But he would never, ever admit that. He had a reputation to maintain. He had to think of something clever.

"Hmph!" he snorted, stalling for time. He remembered his theory about Farmer Green setting traps. And he remembered the talk of maps. An idea, a truly dreadful and exciting idea, popped into his head.

"This," he announced in a grave voice, "is no smiling face. And it is no moon. You are both very foolish. Any one with any experience can see what this is. It is a picture of a _trap_."

"A trap!" Frisky and Sandy exclaimed in one breath.

"Certainly," said Mr. Crow, warming to his story. "It is one of those round, steel traps with teeth. Farmer Green has drawn you a picture of it so you will know what to look for. And he has left you a nut for bait, to show you how he will trick you. It is a warning!"

"A warning?" Sandy asked. "But... but why would he warn me?"

"That--" said Mr. Crow--"that is the cunning of it. He is playing a game with you. He is telling you, 'I am going to set this trap for you, and I dare you to avoid it.' It is a challenge! And the red thread means danger. Great danger!"

Frisky Squirrel's tail bushed out in alarm. Sandy Chipmunk felt a cold shiver run all the way down his back. A trap! A challenge from Farmer Green himself! It was a terrible thought.

"Thank you, Mr. Crow," Sandy said in a small voice. "You have been a great help."

"Of course," Mr. Crow cawed, puffing out his chest again. "Now you know. And you had better tell every one. Farmer Green is on the war-path. No nut is safe!"

XV A FOREST IN A FRIGHT

As you can imagine, that dreadful news spread through the woods and fields even faster than the story about the treasure map. Frisky Squirrel, his heart pounding with fear, scurried off to tell his family. "Farmer Green is setting steel traps everywhere!" he chattered. "He is using nuts for bait, and he leaves a picture of the trap so you know it's his! And the nuts are tied with a red thread of doom!"

The squirrel family told the Rabbit cousins. And the Rabbit cousins, who were frightened of their own shadows, told every one they met. Fatty Coon heard it and decided to stay in his hollow tree all the next day. Even bold Peter Mink, who was afraid of nothing, thought it might be wise to stick close to the river bank.

By sundown, all of Pleasant Valley was in a state of terror. The woods, usually full of the rustle and bustle of busy folk, were strangely silent. No one dared to touch a fallen nut. Every twig that snapped sounded like the clang of a trap.

Sandy Chipmunk was the most miserable of all. He hid deep in his nest, the fine hickory nut lying untouched in the corner. He felt it was all his fault. If he had never meddled with the mail-box, none of this would have happened.

The next morning, Johnnie Green was very disappointed. He had watched from his window, but he had not seen the chipmunk take the nut. "Maybe he didn't see it," he said to himself.

So, on his way to school, he left another present. This time it was a shiny brass button that had fallen off his coat. He placed it right on the flat stone that Sandy used as a porch.

When Sandy finally peeked out of his hole, there was the button, gleaming in the sun. He froze in horror. It was round, just like the drawing. It was made of metal. It must be one of the traps!

He backed into his tunnel, his heart thumping. "He knows where I live!" he whispered. "He's putting the traps right on my doorstep!"

He stayed hidden all day. He was very hungry, for he was now afraid to eat the hickory nut, too. Late in the afternoon, his hunger made him bold. He crept out and scurried to a different part of the stone wall, far from his home, where he had a secret stash of acorns. As he was digging one up, he heard a familiar voice.

"Well, well. If it isn't the fellow who started all the trouble."

It was Mr. Crow.

"It wasn't my fault," Sandy mumbled, his mouth full of acorn.

"You brought the warning," Mr. Crow insisted. "And now look. The whole valley is starving, afraid to pick up a single nut. I myself have not had a decent meal all day. There's a perfectly good field of corn over there, but who dares go near it? It is surely surrounded by those round, metal things."

Sandy Chipmunk looked over at Farmer Green's cornfield. It did look tempting. The stalks were brown, and the ears were heavy. Then he looked toward the farmhouse. He saw Johnnie Green coming out the back door. The boy was carrying a small basket.

Sandy's first instinct was to run and hide. But then his curiosity got the better of him. He stayed perfectly still behind the wall and watched.

Johnnie did not walk toward the woods. Instead, he walked to a new wooden pole that his father had put up near the garden. On top of the pole was a little house with a hole in it. Farmer Green had built it for the bluebirds.

Johnnie reached into his basket and began to fill the little house with something. It was birdseed. Then he scattered some more on the ground around the pole. He waited for a minute, and then two bluebirds flew down and began to peck at the seeds. They flew in and out of the little house, singing happily. They did not seem to be in any danger at all.

Sandy watched, his brow wrinkled in thought. He watched as Johnnie went back to the house. He watched the birds for a long, long time. They were not afraid. There was no trap.

A new idea began to form in Sandy's mind. It was a small idea at first, but it grew and grew. What if the round thing was not a trap? What if the smiling face was not a picture of a trap? What if... what if Mr. Crow had been wrong?

It was a startling thought. Mr. Crow was _always_ so sure of himself. But the more Sandy thought about it, the more sense it made. The bluebirds were safe. Johnnie Green did not look like a wicked trickster; he looked like a boy scattering seeds.

"There is only one way to be sure," Sandy said to himself. And his heart began to beat fast, not with fear this time, but with a kind of nervous courage.

He scurried back to his nest and bravely poked his head out. The brass button was still there. He nudged it. It didn't snap. It didn't bite. It just slid across the stone. He picked it up. It was smooth and cool. It was not a trap at all. It was just a button.

Then he looked at the hickory nut. He untied the red thread and nibbled one end of the nut. It was sweet and delicious. It was not poisoned.

Mr. Crow was wrong. He was completely and utterly wrong.

XVI SANDY THE BRAVE

A great anger rose in Sandy Chipmunk's chest. It was an anger at being so frightened, and at seeing all his neighbors so frightened, all for nothing.

"I must tell them," he declared. "I must tell them the truth."

He took the brass button in his mouth and scampered to the top of the stone wall. "Listen!" he squeaked as loudly as he could. "Every one, listen to me!"

A few heads popped out. Frisky Squirrel peered from a hole in a tree. A rabbit peeked from behind a bush.

"It's a trick!" a voice squawked from above. It was Mr. Crow, swooping down to land on a nearby fence post. "He has one of the traps! He is trying to lure you out! Don't listen to him!"

"It is not a trap!" Sandy cried, dropping the button so they could all see it. "It is a button! Just a plain, ordinary button! And the nut was not poisoned! It was a good nut!"

"Lies!" cawed Mr. Crow. "He is working for Farmer Green! He has turned traitor!"

The woodsfolk ducked back into their hiding places, confused and afraid. They did not know whom to believe. Sandy was their friend, but Mr. Crow was old and sounded so very certain.

Sandy knew he had to do something more. Words were not enough. He had to show them. He remembered the cornfield, and the bluebirds, and Johnnie Green. He had a daring plan.

"Follow me!" he shouted. "If you are brave enough, follow me and I will show you the truth!"

He leaped from the wall and ran, not toward the deep woods, but out into the open, straight for Farmer Green's garden and the new bluebird house. Mr. Crow and a few of the bolder animals followed at a distance, hiding behind trees and bushes, to see what would happen.

Sandy did not hesitate. He ran right up to the pole of the birdhouse. He could smell the fresh seed. His heart was in his throat, but he kept going. He scrambled up the wooden pole, just as he would climb a tree.

"He's done for now!" Mr. Crow whispered to Jasper Jay, who was shivering on a branch beside him. "It's a trap for birds and chipmunks alike!"

Sandy reached the little house. He crept onto its roof and looked down. Below, he could see the scared faces of his friends, peeking out from their hiding spots. He took a deep breath. Then he hopped down onto the little platform by the entrance hole and boldly stuck his head inside.

He grabbed a big, striped sunflower seed, one of "Chipmunk's Choice," in fact. He backed out and held it up for all to see. Then, sitting there on the platform of the birdhouse, in full view of Farmer Green's kitchen window, he ate it.

A great, collective gasp went up from the woods. They waited. They watched.

Nothing happened. Sandy Chipmunk did not fall over. The house did not snap shut on him. He simply finished his seed, wiped his whiskers, and took another.

A cheer went up from the squirrels. The rabbits thumped their feet in applause. One by one, the animals came out of hiding, their faces full of relief and wonder.

Sandy Chipmunk had been right. It was not a trap. It was a bird feeder.

All eyes turned to Mr. Crow. He sat on his fence post, his feathers ruffled. He looked from the cheering crowd to Sandy, who was now happily stuffing his cheeks with seeds. Mr. Crow had never felt so foolish in his entire life. He had been wrong about the letter, and now he had been wrong about the trap. He had frightened the entire valley for no reason at all.

Without a single _caw_ or a boast or a sneer, he spread his black wings and flew away, over the trees and out of sight.

That evening, the woods were once again full of happy sounds. The animals feasted on the nuts they had been too afraid to touch. Sandy Chipmunk, a hero, sat on his doorstep, polishing his shiny brass button. He had learned a great many things. He had learned that stories change in the telling. He had learned that the oldest and loudest person is not always the wisest.

And most important of all, he had learned that it is a fine thing to receive a letter, but it is an even finer thing to find out the truth for yourself.

XIII A THIEF IN THE VALLEY

For a time, a great peace settled over Pleasant Valley. Without Mr. Crow's loud _caws_ and his even louder opinions, the woods seemed strangely quiet. At first, the animals enjoyed the silence. They went about their business of gathering nuts and seeds for the winter, and no one told them they were doing it wrong. Frisky Squirrel was quite sure Mr. Crow had flown south for good, and he told every one so.
"He was so ashamed," Frisky would chatter from a branch, "that he has gone to live with the buzzards. I am certain of it. We shall never see him again."
Sandy Chipmunk was not so sure. He remembered the look on Mr. Crow's face, a look not of anger, but of deep embarrassment. And Sandy felt a little sorry for him. After all, Mr. Crow had only been mistaken; and being mistaken, Sandy was beginning to learn, was something that could happen to any one, even a very clever chipmunk.
But the days grew shorter and colder, and soon there was a new trouble in Pleasant Valley. It began in a small way. One morning, Mrs. Rabbit came weeping from her cozy home in the briar patch.
"My pretty blue glass is gone!" she sobbed to any one who would listen. "It was a piece of a bottle that I found near the road, and it shone in the sun like a piece of the sky. I kept it right on my doorstep, and now it has vanished!"
No one thought much of it, for things are often lost in the woods. But the very next day, Jasper Jay let out a furious squawk from the top of a hickory tree.
"My button!" he shrieked. "My best shiny button! It was a brass one from one of Farmer Green's old coats. I had it woven right into the side of my nest, and now some thief has pulled it out!"
After that, the complaints came quickly. Fatty Coon discovered that a lovely, crinkly piece of tin-foil was missing from his hollow log. One of the Red-Squirrel boys could not find a little silver bell he had taken from a cat's collar long ago. Every one had lost something. And every missing thing had one thing in common: it was small, and it was shiny.
It did not take long for the talk to begin. And as usual, it was Frisky Squirrel who helped it along.
"It's Mr. Crow!" he announced, his tail twitching with excitement. "I know it is! He is angry with us all for laughing at him. He is sneaking back at night and stealing our treasures for revenge!"
The story grew, just as the story of the mail-box had grown. Soon, every one was saying that Mr. Crow had become a wicked robber. They said he had a secret cave filled with stolen goods, and that he sat there all day, laughing his terrible _haw-haw_ laugh. The younger animals were told to stay inside their homes after dusk, for fear the great black thief would swoop down and snatch them.
The valley, which had been so peaceful, was now full of fear once more. Doors were barred and nuts were hidden away, even though the thief had never once taken a single bite of food.
Sandy Chipmunk heard the stories, and he shook his head. He remembered how Mr. Crow had wanted corn, and only corn. He remembered how Mr. Crow had sneered at the idea of taking a letter that was not his. It did not seem like Mr. Crow to steal buttons and bits of glass. A boaster he was, and a bully, too. But a thief? Sandy was not so sure.
"It is just like the bird feeder," he said to himself, sitting on his own doorstep. "Every one is telling a story, but no one has seen the truth. I think I shall have to go and look for it again."

XIV SANDY PLAYS DETECTIVE

Sandy Chipmunk began his work at once. He did not run about telling every one his opinion. Instead, he visited the animals who had lost their treasures. First, he went to Jasper Jay, who was still complaining bitterly.
"It was the shiniest button in the whole valley," Jasper grumbled. "It took me a week to work it loose from that old coat. And for a crow to come and steal it--it is an outrage!"
"Did you see Mr. Crow take it, Jasper?" Sandy asked quietly.
"Well--no," Jasper Jay admitted. "I did not _see_ him. But who else could it be? He loves shiny things. Every one knows that."
Sandy knew that was true. Mr. Crow did like things that glittered. But that was not proof.
Next, he visited Mrs. Rabbit in her briar patch. She was still quite sad about her bit of blue glass.
"It happened in the night," she told Sandy. "I am a very light sleeper, but I heard nothing at all. Not a single _caw_. Not a single flap of a wing."
"That is very strange," Sandy said, stroking his whiskers thoughtfully. "Mr. Crow is not known for being quiet."
He talked to Fatty Coon and to the Red-Squirrel boy and to a field mouse who had lost a small piece of a broken mirror. And every one told the same story. The shiny object was there one evening and gone the next morning. And no one had seen or heard the thief.
Sandy sat upon a stone wall to think. The thief was silent. The thief worked at night or very early in the morning. And the thief took only shiny things, not food. It seemed to Sandy Chipmunk that Mr. Crow was not a good fit for such a thief. Mr. Crow was noisy. And Mr. Crow was always, always interested in food.
"There is another story here," Sandy said to himself. "And I do not think Mr. Crow is the villain in it."
But what was he to do? He could not watch every nest and burrow in the valley all at once. He needed a plan. And he needed help.
He went to find Frisky Squirrel, who was busy telling a group of young rabbits about Mr. Crow's mountain of stolen jewels.
"Frisky," Sandy said, pulling him aside. "I need to speak with you."
"Is it about Mr. Crow?" Frisky asked eagerly. "Have you heard that he now has a crown made of bottle caps?"
"No," Sandy replied patiently. "It is about the thief. I do not think it is Mr. Crow."
Frisky Squirrel's jaw dropped. "Not Mr. Crow? But who else could it be? Every one says--"
"And every one said the bird feeder was a trap," Sandy reminded him gently. "Remember? You and I were afraid, too. But we were wrong. We believed a story without looking for the truth."
Frisky shuffled his feet. He remembered that day very well. He remembered how foolish he had felt.
"What are you going to do?" he asked in a much quieter voice.
"I am going to catch the thief," Sandy announced. "Or, at least, I am going to see who the thief is. And I want you to help me. We will set a trap."
Frisky's eyes grew wide. "A trap! But we can't! What if we hurt some one?"
"Not that sort of trap," Sandy explained. "A watching-trap. We will put something very shiny out in the open. Then we will hide and watch it. When the thief comes to take it, we will see who it is. Then the true story can be told."
Frisky Squirrel thought about this. It sounded very exciting. He would be the first to know the truth, besides Sandy. And he could be the one to tell every one the real story.
"All right," he said, his tail giving a happy flick. "I will help you. What shall we use for bait?"
Sandy looked around. His sharp eyes spotted something gleaming under a fern near the road. It was the metal top from a ginger-ale bottle, round and silvery with a bit of red paint on it.
"That," said Sandy Chipmunk, "is perfect."

XV THE WATCH ON THE STUMP

That evening, just as the sun was setting behind the hills, Sandy Chipmunk and Frisky Squirrel put their plan into action. They chose a spot carefully: a large, flat-topped stump in a clearing, not too far into the woods but not too close to any one's home. It was a place many animals passed by each day.
With great care, Sandy placed the shiny bottle top right in the middle of the stump. It caught the last rays of the sun and winked like a tiny star.
"Now we hide," Sandy whispered.
They found a perfect hiding spot in a thick clump of ferns a short distance away. From there, they had a clear view of the stump, but they themselves were completely hidden.
And so they waited. The woods grew dark and quiet. A pale moon rose over the trees, casting long, strange shadows. Frisky Squirrel began to grow nervous.
"What if it _is_ Mr. Crow?" he whispered, his teeth chattering. "He will be very angry that we have tricked him."
"If it is Mr. Crow," Sandy whispered back, "then we will know the truth. And knowing the truth is always better than being afraid of a story. Now, be quiet."
An hour went by. A rabbit hopped through the clearing, nibbled at a bit of clover, and hopped on, paying no mind to the bottle top. Later, Fatty Coon ambled past, sniffing the air for any sign of a late-night snack. He glanced at the stump, saw that the shiny object was not edible, and continued on his way.
Frisky was beginning to get tired. His eyes were drooping. "Perhaps the thief is not coming tonight," he yawned.
"We must wait a little longer," Sandy insisted. His own eyes were bright and alert. He was determined to solve the mystery.
They sat in silence for what seemed like a very long time. The moon was high in the sky now. Suddenly, Sandy nudged Frisky with his paw.
"Look," he breathed.
There was a flicker of movement in the branches of a tall pine tree at the edge of the clearing. It was not the large, slow flap of a crow's wing. It was a quick, jerky motion.
A bird flew down from the pine tree and landed silently on the stump. In the moonlight, they could see it was not black, but a handsome dark blue and white. It was a Blue Jay. But it was not their neighbor, Jasper Jay. This one was younger and a bit smaller.
The Blue Jay hopped around the bottle top, turning his head from side to side and looking at it with his bright, black eyes. He seemed very pleased with it. After a moment of admiration, he picked it up neatly in his beak, and with a silent flick of his wings, he flew back up toward the top of the very same pine tree from which he had come.
Sandy and Frisky looked at each other, their eyes wide with surprise.
"A Blue Jay!" Frisky whispered. "It was not Mr. Crow at all!"
"Hush!" Sandy said. "Let us follow him. We must see where he has taken it."
They crept from their hiding place and scurried to the base of the tall pine tree. It was much too high for them to climb all the way to the top. But Sandy was a clever chipmunk. He shinnied up a smaller maple tree that grew beside the pine. From a high branch on the maple, he could just peer into a large, messy nest of twigs near the top of the pine.
And what he saw made him gasp.
The nest was decorated with dozens and dozens of shiny things. There was Jasper's brass button, and a piece of blue glass that surely belonged to Mrs. Rabbit. There was Fatty Coon's tin-foil, and the Red-Squirrel's silver bell, and countless other bits of metal, broken crockery, and glittering stones. And in the middle of it all, the young Blue Jay was carefully tucking away the ginger-ale bottle top he had just taken from the stump.
Sandy scrambled back down the tree to where Frisky was waiting anxiously.
"You were right, Frisky," Sandy said, though he did not look happy. "It was not Mr. Crow."
"Who was it?" Frisky demanded.
"It was another jay," Sandy explained. "A young one. His nest is full of all the missing things. He is not a thief for revenge. He just... likes things that shine."
Frisky Squirrel sat back on his haunches. He thought of all the terrible stories he had told about Mr. Crow. He thought of how frightened all the little animals were. And he felt his cheeks grow hot with shame.
"Oh, dear," he said in a very small voice. "We have made another mistake. A very big one."

XVI A CROW'S RETURN

The next morning, the news spread through Pleasant Valley, but this time it was the true story. Sandy and Frisky went together from burrow to den to nest, and they told every one what they had seen.
They led a small group, including Jasper Jay and Mrs. Rabbit, to the tall pine tree. The young Blue Jay, whose name turned out to be Jimmy, was very frightened when he was discovered. He confessed at once that he had taken all the things.
"I did not mean any harm!" he chirped, shivering in his nest. "They were just so pretty! They sparkle in the sun! I was making my nest beautiful."
Jasper Jay looked at his button, then at the frightened young bird. He was not nearly so angry now. "He is only a foolish young fellow," Jasper said. "Not a wicked villain."
All the animals agreed that Jimmy Jay must return every single thing he had taken. And they all agreed that they had been very foolish themselves, to blame Mr. Crow without a shred of proof.
They were standing in the clearing, watching as Jimmy Jay began the long work of returning his treasures, when a long, dark shadow fell over them.
A great black bird landed on the branch of a dead chestnut tree nearby. He was silent. He did not _caw_ or boast. His feathers seemed less glossy than before, and he looked thinner and very tired.
It was Mr. Crow.
A hush fell over the animals. No one knew what to say. They looked at the ground and shuffled their feet. Frisky Squirrel tried to hide behind Fatty Coon.
Mr. Crow looked at the group of animals. He looked at the shamefaced young Blue Jay flying down with a piece of mirror in his beak. Then his sharp eyes settled on Sandy Chipmunk.
"So," Mr. Crow said, and his voice was not a sneer, but a low, raspy croak. "You have found your thief."
Sandy took a brave step forward. "Yes, Mr. Crow, we have."
"I heard the stories," Mr. Crow went on, his gaze sweeping over the crowd. "I was not far away. Just in the deep woods. I heard that I was a robber. I heard that I had a cave full of jewels." He paused. "I suppose you were all very pleased to have a villain to blame for your troubles."
The animals felt even more ashamed. It was true. It had been easy to blame the one who was not there.
It was Sandy Chipmunk who spoke. His voice was clear and steady.

A WINTER FEAST

They were not the playful flakes that had hurried the animals in their work; these were thick, heavy sheets of white that fell without stopping for two whole days. For they knew that the hollow log at the edge of the woods was filled to bursting with golden corn.

And every morning, no matter how the wind howled, he would fly from his high pine to the hollow log. There he would meet Sandy Chipmunk, and together they would hand out the day's rations.

"A good morning to you, Mrs. Rabbit," Mr. Crow would say, his voice no longer sneering, but business-like. "Here are eight kernels for your family. Be sure to tell your little ones not to eat them all at once."

"Frisky Squirrel!" he would call out. "You and your cousins get ten kernels today for your excellent work on the cobs. Do try not to bury any of them and forget where they are."

Frisky would chatter his thanks and scamper off, his tail twitching with delight.

Even those who had done little work received something. "Here, Jasper Jay," Mr. Crow said one morning, dropping a single, perfect kernel before the noisy blue jay. "This is for... well, for not getting in the way too much."

Jasper Jay snatched the kernel and flew off, squawking that he certainly deserved more, but no one paid him much mind.

His curiosity was now much stronger than his fear. He scurried up the side of the barn to a place where a board was missing, making a perfect little window. Peeking through the gap, he could see the whole scene below.

There was the machine. It was a big wooden thing with a giant wheel on the side. And Johnnie Green was turning the wheel. He was not groaning in anger; in fact, he was whistling a cheerful tune. Farmer Green was there, too, and he was dumping baskets of red and yellow apples into a hopper at the top of the machine.

With every turn of the wheel, the apples were crunched and mashed inside the machine. And a thick, brown liquid was pouring out of a spout at the bottom, right into a big wooden barrel. The whole barn was filled with that wonderful, sweet smell.

Sandy watched for a long time. He saw Farmer Green take a cup, hold it under the spout, and fill it with the brown juice. Then Farmer Green lifted the cup to his lips and took a long drink. He did not make a sour face. He did not spit it out. Instead, he smiled a wide, happy smile and said something to Johnnie, who laughed and took a drink himself.

Sandy Chipmunk's little heart was filled with relief. He knew, now, without a doubt. Mr. Crow had been wrong again. This was no Punishment Machine. This was a machine for making something good. It was an Apple-Juice Machine!

He was so pleased with his discovery that he almost chattered aloud. He had found out the truth all by himself! And the truth was not frightening at all; it was sweet-smelling and interesting.

He watched until Farmer Green and his son finished their work, covered the barrel, and went back to the house for their supper. Then Sandy crept down from his hiding place. On the floor of the barn, near the great machine, was a small puddle where some of the juice had spilled.

Very cautiously, Sandy crept over to it. He sniffed. The smell was even more wonderful up close. He dipped one tiny paw into the puddle and then licked it.

It was delicious! It was sweet and tangy and tasted more like apples than apples themselves. It was the best thing he had ever tasted in his life. He quickly lapped up the entire puddle, until not a single drop was left.

"A Punishment Machine, indeed!" he said to himself with a chuckle. "I'd like a punishment like that every day!"

He scampered back to the stone wall, his mind buzzing. He had to tell the others. He had to let them know that Mr. Crow had been telling them another one of his grand, foolish stories. And Sandy knew just how he was going to do it.

XV
A TASTE OF THE TRUTH

When Sandy Chipmunk got back to the woods, he found a worried group of animals gathered near the big hickory tree. They were all talking in low, anxious voices about the terrible Punishment Machine.

"I hear it can grind up nuts as well as apples," Jasper Jay was saying.

"And I heard," whispered Fatty Coon, "that Farmer Green is going to put pepper in the next batch, to make it even worse!"

Just then, Mr. Crow flew down from his tree. He looked very smug.

"Well," he said, clearing his throat. "I trust you have all decided to be good and stay away from the barn. It is a good thing you have me to warn you of these dangers."

"It is not a danger at all!" a small voice piped up.

Every one turned. It was Sandy Chipmunk, standing on a large stone with his paws on his hips.

Mr. Crow glared at him. "What foolishness are you talking now, little chipmunk?" he demanded. "Did you not hear my warning? I have seen the machine with my own eyes!"

"And so have I," Sandy announced bravely. "I have just come from the barn. And it is not a Punishment Machine. It is a machine for making apple juice!"

A gasp went through the crowd.

"Apple juice!" Mr. Crow sneered, laughing a harsh _haw-haw_ that had no fun in it at all. "The boy is mad! He has eaten a bad nut and it has gone to his head. Do you think Farmer Green would go to all that trouble just to make juice?"

"But he was drinking it!" Sandy insisted. "And so was Johnnie Green! And they were smiling! And it smelled sweet, not sour!"

The other animals looked from Sandy to Mr. Crow, and back again. They did not know who to believe. Sandy's story sounded very pleasant, but Mr. Crow's story had been so much more exciting and frightening.

"He is trying to trick you!" Mr. Crow cawed loudly. "He wants you all to go to the barn so you will be caught! He is working for Farmer Green!"

This was a terrible accusation, and Sandy's face grew hot with anger. "I am not!" he cried. "I am telling you the truth! And I can prove it!"

"Prove it?" Mr. Crow scoffed. "And how do you propose to do that? Are you going to bring the whole machine here for us to see?"

"No," said Sandy, his voice steady. "I am going to bring you a taste of the truth."

And with that, he turned and scampered away, back toward the barn, leaving a very confused crowd of animals behind him. Even Mr. Crow was silent for a moment, wondering what the little chipmunk could possibly mean.

Sandy knew he had to be quick. He ran along the stone wall as fast as his legs would carry him. He needed something to carry the juice in. As he neared the barn, he saw it: a single large acorn cup, left behind from the day before. It was just the thing!

He crept back into the barn. It was dark and quiet now. The big barrel of juice stood in the corner, covered with a wooden lid. The lid was too heavy for him to move. But he remembered the spout. He pushed the acorn cup under the spout, but nothing came out. Then he saw that the spout had a small wooden handle, or a spigot, sticking out of its side.

He climbed up and pushed on the handle with all his might. It would not move. He pushed again, bracing his feet against the spout. Suddenly, the handle turned. A tiny trickle of the dark, sweet juice flowed out and into his acorn cup. He quickly turned the handle back before more than a few drops could spill.

His heart thumping with success, he carefully picked up the full acorn cup with his teeth and scurried out of the barn. It was hard work, carrying the cup without spilling it, and he had to go very slowly.

When he finally got back to the hickory tree, all the animals were still there, waiting. Mr. Crow was pacing back and forth on a branch, looking impatient.

"Here," Sandy said, setting the acorn cup down carefully on the stone. "Here is the juice from the machine. I told you it was not sour."

The animals all crowded around, peering into the tiny cup. It was filled with a brown liquid that shimmered in the fading light. A sweet, spicy smell rose from it.

"It smells good," Fatty Coon said wistfully. "It does not smell like punishment at all."

"It is a trick!" Mr. Crow squawked from his branch. "It is poison! He has brought you poison to drink! Do not touch it!"

The animals backed away nervously.

Sandy looked up at Mr. Crow. "You are a coward," he said plainly. "You are afraid of being wrong again. If it is poison, why does it smell so sweet? And if it is a Punishment Machine, why did I see Farmer Green drink it and smile?"

Then he did a very brave thing. He dipped his own paw into the acorn cup and licked it. "Mmm," he said loudly. "It is even better than before."

Frisky Squirrel, who was Sandy's friend, crept a little closer. He was frightened, but he trusted Sandy more than he trusted Mr. Crow. "Is it really good?" he whispered.

"It is wonderful," Sandy said. "Try some."

Very timidly, Frisky dipped the very tip of his nose into the cup. His whiskers twitched. Then he took a tiny lick.

His eyes opened wide. "It is good!" he chattered. "It is sweet! It tastes like sunshine and apples!"

That was all the encouragement the others needed. Fatty Coon pushed forward and took a big slurp. Jasper Jay flew down and dipped his beak in. Soon, every one was crowding around, trying to get a tiny taste of the wonderful apple juice. There were cries of "Delicious!" and "Wonderful!" and "More!"

All the while, Mr. Crow sat on his branch, his feathers ruffled in anger and shame. He watched as every single animal tasted the juice and declared it to be the finest thing they had ever had. His grand story of the Punishment Machine had crumbled into nothing, just like his story of the Wood-Gobbler. He had been proven wrong. Again. And this time, every one had the proof right on their own tongues.

He could not bear their happy chatter. He could not bear the triumphant look on Sandy Chipmunk's face. He had tried to win back his importance with a lie, and the lie had been uncovered by a simple taste of the truth.

Without a single word, without even a croak of defiance, he spread his black wings and flew away. He did not fly to his high perch. He flew deep, deep into the woods, far away from the sounds of laughter at the hickory tree. And this time, the other animals did not even watch him go. They were too busy trying to get the last drop of apple juice from Sandy's little acorn cup.

Sandy Chipmunk looked at his friends, all happy and excited, and he felt very proud. Not because he had been right, but because he had helped them see the truth for themselves. And he knew, as he watched Frisky Squirrel try to tip the acorn cup up for one last taste, that a small cup of truth was worth more than a whole forest full of exciting lies.
